blocks.text: Once generated, the simulation environments can be used for many different applications. We first quantify the utility of our simulation suite by comparing the outcomes of GR00T 2 policy evaluations in sim and in real (Sec. J.2.1). We then highlight how these high-fidelity environments contributed to GR00T 2 development, including: optimization of GR00T 2 inference for deployment (Sec. J.2.2), faster iteration on the GR00T 2 pretraining process (Sec. J.2.3), and the development of agentic recovery skills in simulation that assist GR00T 2 during real-world deployment (Sec. J.2.4).

blocks.text: J.2.1. Sim and Real Policy Evaluation Correlation Analysis
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: In order for our simulation suite to be useful, it is important for simulation to be calibrated with the real world. In this section, we gauge our simulation quality by seeing if it can be used as convincing surrogate for real world evaluation (Ranawaka et al., 2026; Jain et al., 2025). We test our policies zero-shot in simulation, without additional fine-tuning or co-training with simulation data, and find that the simulation evaluations strongly correlate with real-world results. This enables the testing of policies at a scale, cadence, and level of reproducibility that would be intractable for real-world evals.
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: Setup. We evaluate 14 checkpoints in both simulation and the real world on matched setups across 25 tasks on the YAM embodiment. Additionally, we evaluate 10 tasks on the DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) embodiment with 5 generalist checkpoints. Each task is evaluated for 5 trials on the real robots, and 10 trials in simulation.
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: Metrics. We measure sim and real correlation using Pearson Correlation Coefficient (r), Spearman Rank Correlation Coefficient (𝜌) and the Mean Maximum Rank Violation (MMRV) proposed by Li et al. (2024). For a simulation that perfectly reflects real-world conditions, we would observe 𝑟→1, indicating that policy performance in simulation matches that in the real world, 𝜌→1, indicating that the relative rankings of policies are maintained between simulation and the real world, and MMRV →0, indicating that the number of policy ranking violations are minimized. blocks.text: Bradley-Terry (BT) (Bradley and Terry, 1952) Elo ratings of the checkpoints. Task progress is the rubric score of a trial, a weighted sum of the completed sub-tasks between 0 and 1, and a trial is successful when the score is 1. Both are averaged within each task and then across tasks. MMRV is reported for task progress and success rate.
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: Bradley-Terry Elo. Real-world evaluations use blinded A/B tests: in each trial, two or three checkpoints run in randomized order from the same initial setup (based on a corresponding simulation initialization), and every pair of checkpoints in the trial forms one comparison, won by the higher score (equal scores count as a tie). We fit BT ratings to these pairwise outcomes. In simulation, every checkpoint is evaluated on the same fixed initial layouts (10 per task), so any two checkpoints can be compared layout by layout without re-running them.
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: Results on YAM embodiment. We evaluate 14 GR00T 2 variants across 25 YAM tasks in the same simulator. We completed real-world trials with the A/B evaluation procedure defined earlier. For each trial, we aligned the object initialization with the simulation using projected overlays. We find that our simulator predicts policy performance with high correlations with the real world, with a Pearson 𝑟up to 0.93 for task progress and BT Elo score. Since evaluations in both the real world and simulation can be non-deterministic, and the number of trials per task is limited, there is an effective statistical ceiling to how high these correlations can be for even a perfect simulator. Following Lage-Castellanos et al. (2019), we estimate this ceiling by assuming a perfect simulator. blocks.text: Results on DROID embodiment. Separately, we evaluate five generalist DROID checkpoints including GR00T 2 and publicly available models on environments reconstructed from real-world DROID setups. We use the same five layouts per task for each checkpoint in the real-world and the same ten layouts in simulation, to minimize variation in trial initializations. Once again, we see high Pearson r of 0.98, 0.95, 0.97 for task progress, success rate and BT Elo respectively. This demonstrates that our agentic real-to-sim reconstruction method is viable for different embodiments.

blocks.text: J.2.2. GR00T 2 Inference Optimization through Simulation
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: Inference optimization aims to help GR00T 2 respond sooner to new observations while preserving task success and smooth motion. We optimize model execution and the processing and transfer of observations, and vary the number of steps used to refine video and action predictions (see Accelerating Model Inference). Simulation provides a repeatable setting for testing how these changes affect behavior. We can restart each trial from the same scene without repeatedly setting up a physical workcell, making it practical to screen settings before robot testing.
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: Changes that reduce prediction time can also change action predictions, so task success and motion quality must be checked together. For each checkpoint, we keep the number of actions per prediction fixed while comparing original PyTorch execution with TensorRT and CUDA Graphs and testing different numbers of refinement steps. In a YAM cube-handover pilot, several settings completed the task but differed in motion smoothness. Follow-up trials of the same checkpoint and task on a physical YAM robot also showed this distinction. In separate runtime comparisons, the optimized implementation supported more frequent updates to the action plan with comparable task progress in simulation.
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: Simulation also helps us prototype real-time chunking (RTC), which connects new action predictions to actions already scheduled for execution. In separate simulation experiments (see Policy Smoothness), we compare RTC training with and without noise added to the previous action sequence. Repeated trials from matched scenes with controlled prediction delays help us assess whether smoother transitions between action sequences preserve task success, without testing every delay setting on physical robots.
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: We measure prediction latency directly on the target hardware, separately from simulated task duration. Ordinary synchronous simulation pauses while waiting for predictions, so it does not reproduce the effect of inference delay on a moving robot. The RTC experiments explicitly model this delay, but physical-robot tests remain necessary to check behavior under actual deployment timing. Simulation narrows the settings taken to these tests, where we assess task success and motion quality on the target robot.
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: J.2.3. GR00T 2 Pretraining Acceleration with Simulation
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: Simulation enabled faster iteration on GR00T 2 pretraining through many different means.
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: Monitoring of pretraining progress and checkpoint selection. Evaluating a single pretraining checkpoint across a large set of real-world tasks can take hours. Simulation provides a faster way to compare policies across a diverse task set during model development. During GR00T 2 pretraining, we evaluated intermediate checkpoints on a set of tasks from our simulation suite to inspect their closed-loop behavior and compare model capabilities as training progressed. These comparisons help us identify overfitting as we iterate on the model, and assess the relative performance of our checkpoints and external baselines without running extensive real-world evaluations for every candidate.
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: Simulation also guided checkpoint selection: we used a subset of our simulation suite (25 tasks) to determine which checkpoints showed promising closed-loop evaluation results. This provided a stable way to understand if checkpoints were worth physical robot evaluation. As a concrete example, we used this workflow to finalize our pretrained model: simulation results narrowed the candidates to three checkpoints, which we then evaluated on physical robots to select the final checkpoint. In this way, simulation was a tool to guide checkpoint analysis and development, but we still used physical-robot evaluation to validate conclusions about real-world performance.
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: Optimizing the data pipeline. Changes to the data loading and processing pipeline are costly to assess through full-scale pretraining. We expect a new pipeline that processes the data correctly and preserves training dynamics to produce model performance comparable to the existing pipeline. We test this expectation with small-scale training and closed-loop simulation before adopting a new pipeline for pretraining.
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: As an example, we compared five configurations that varied sequence packing, mixed-shard sampling, and text-token masking. For each configuration, we post-trained a model on real-robot teleoperation data from the YAM Scoop and Unscrew tasks, then evaluated it on simulated versions of those tasks. Simulation was used only for evaluation. The new data loading pipeline showed no observed regression in closed-loop simulation performance relative to the existing pipeline, giving us confidence to adopt it for pretraining.
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: J.2.4. Agentic Skill Development in Simulation
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation

blocks.text: Simulation also helps us develop specialized manipulation skills. As described in Sec. G.1, ASPIRE learns skills that code-as-policy (CaP) can invoke alongside GR00T 2 to carry out difficult steps or recover from failures. For example, the toy plane assembly task (Fig. 64) provided a repeatable setting for developing recovery skills that transferred to physical robots. In simulation, we could test candidate behaviors, inspect failures, and refine the skills before evaluating them on the physical system.
blocks.section: J.2. Accelerating GR00T 2 Development with Simulation
